extracted: Notifications for 2007–2009: 822 in the CDR under the EMCDDA definition and 562 in the police registry, together 929 people. Only 455 (49%) were in both; 367 (40%) were in the CDR count only; 74 (8%) were in the police registry with a CDR cause of death outside the EMCDDA definition; 33 (4%) police-registry deaths had no CDR match (39% of them not Norwegian citizens, the rest with missing or erroneous ID numbers). Compared with deaths in both, deaths in the CDR count only were older (mean 42.7 against 35.3 years) and more often had dependence or suicide as the cause (33% against 8%); in the adjusted model morphine/codeine (odds ratio 6.89), methadone (3.69), synthetic opioids (4.63) and stimulants (2.36, 95% interval 1.16–4.76) against heroin, no autopsy (2.66) and death in a hospital or other institution (2.61) went with being in the CDR count only. An autopsy was recorded for 715 of the 822 CDR deaths. The author states that neither police reporting nor the CDR/EMCDDA count should be considered the correct figure for drug deaths in Norway. The Table 1 first-drug comparison uses the first contributing-cause T-code in the CDR and first mentioned drug in police data. The CDR covered Norwegian residents only, whereas police covered all unnatural deaths regardless of residency. After warning that neither figure is correct, the author judges CDR figures more complete and broader and both probably too low.

Poisoning deaths of New Mexico residents, 1995–1998: 1,046 in vital statistics, 1,046 in OMI records, 987 in both and 1,105 in either (each source alone 94.7%, both 89.3%); only vital statistics held residents who died in another state. Of 59 vital-statistics poisonings not classed as poisonings by the OMI, 24 occurred out of state; of the other 35, 13 were never reported to the OMI and 15 were natural deaths in the OMI database (for example cirrhosis, sepsis or heart disease) that vital statistics attributed to code 305. Of 59 OMI poisonings not classed as poisonings in vital statistics, 37 were coded as natural deaths, typically with poisoning mentioned in Part II but not Part I of the certificate, and 17 as other injury deaths. The poisoning definition includes alcohol, carbon monoxide and other non-drug agents. The use/abuse explanation for code 305 is an inference from the Methods coding rule, not a presented review of the text of each of the 15 certificates.

locator: Case Definitions › 1. Drug-Caused Death, 1-a. Drug Poisoning Death and 2. Drug-Detected Death; Determination and Documentation of Causality, 10th to 12th paragraphs and 19th to 21st paragraphs (Case 3)
extracted: A US consensus panel convened and funded by SAMHSA defined a drug-caused death (certified as resulting from exposure to a drug, alone or with other substances, whatever the intent; parallel to the NCHS drug-induced category), a drug-poisoning death (acute exposure, the lay idea of an overdose; ICD-10 underlying cause X40–X44, X60–X64, X85 or Y10–Y14) and a drug-detected death (a drug found on post-mortem testing whatever its role, including natural and trauma deaths; no ICD-10 equivalent). In its Case 3, a man shot in the head while selling cocaine, with a lethal concentration of a drug, is certified as death from gunshot wounds: drug-detected, not drug-caused. Wording decides the code: 'acute cocaine intoxication', 'cocaine poisoning' or 'cocaine overdose' is coded as poisoning (X42 with T40.5), whereas 'cocaine use' or 'cocaine abuse' is coded to F14 (mental and behavioural disorders due to cocaine).

locator: Methods including ONS and data analysis (p. 2); Results/Fig. 1 (pp. 2–3); Table 1 and strengths/weaknesses (p. 4); abstract (p. 1)
extracted: The National Programme on Substance Use Mortality (NPSUM) receives voluntary reports from over 90% of coroners in England and Wales, with the cause of death and the full toxicology report. For each opioid and year, NPSUM deaths were split into those with the opioid named as a cause and those with an ambiguous drug-related cause in which the consulting toxicologist implicated the opioid, and ONS counts were divided by the named share, without linking individual deaths. In 2011, 122 of 416 NPSUM heroin/morphine deaths (29.3%) had ambiguous causes, and the 574 ONS deaths became a projected 813; in 2022, ONS 1,264 against a projected 1,980 (36% not counted). 2011–2022, ONS count against projected total (share not counted): heroin/morphine 13,471 against 20,323 (34%); methadone 5,752 against 9,444 (39%); tramadol 2,455 against 3,865 (36%); dihydrocodeine 1,201 against 1,854 (35%); codeine 1,886 against 2,859 (34%); fentanyl 599 against 887 (32%). 96.8% (16,101 of 16,628) of the NPSUM opioid-related deaths had multiple drugs detected. ONS searches cause-of-death fields in the Record of Inquest, not its separate conclusion entry. Heroin and morphine are combined. Table 1 Wilson 95% intervals for projected heroin/morphine counts: 2011 813 (767–868), 2022 1,980 (1,894–2,074), all years 20,323 (19,382–21,358). The abstract gives 765–866 for 2011 and the Results 1,895–2,075 for 2022, unlike Table 1; Table 1 values are used here. These intervals reflect sampling error in NPSUM proportions, not representativeness, unlinked projection or causality assumptions. The endpoint ambiguous shares are not the full annual range. Reports from over 90% of coroners do not mean complete case coverage.

locator: 2.1 The NP-SAD database and 2.2 Case identification (p. 68); 2.3 Case categorisation (pp. 68–69); 3.2 Causes of death, 1st paragraph (p. 69); Table 1, column headings (p. 70)
extracted: Of 1,037 accidental drug-related deaths that coroners in England and Wales reported to NP-SAD in 2000 (suicide verdicts, open verdicts with clear intent and deaths without a verdict excluded), two researchers, with a medical consultant confirming, classed 802 (77%) as direct acute overdose; the others were traumatic accidents (31), toxicity with a non-drug-related medical condition (40), toxicity with a drug-related medical condition (72), acute infections (18) and acute non-traumatic physical events, mostly aspiration of stomach contents (74). No comparison with official statistics or ICD codes was made; negative toxicology findings were not recorded. Direct overdose was the default if recent drug use was reported and no other cause suggested, so the authors call 77% an upper limit. The 74 physical-event deaths were mostly aspiration, not all 74; medical-condition deaths and infections were separate categories, not all sudden physical events. Editors' sum of the medical-condition groups is 40+72=112; 802/1,037=77.3%. This is classification of a broader register, not a measured official-overdose false-positive rate.

Second-hand in the scoping review: Quast 2020 compared Florida Medical Examiners Commission and NVSS multiple-cause counts for 2003–2017. Table 2 reports smaller NVSS counts, sizeable gaps for benzodiazepines and opioids, less for amphetamines; at the end the cocaine gap was large while the methadone gap narrowed. The review is therefore evidence that stimulant comparisons exist, not a primary-source confirmation or a validated universal causal miss rate. Quast primary text was not read here.

For 2011 the abstract gives 765–866, whereas Table 1/Results give 767–868; for 2022 the Results give 1,895–2,075 instead of Table 1. These intervals cover sampling error in NPSUM shares, not their representativeness for all deaths or causal accuracy. locator: Results › 2.3.2 Misclassification of heroin-involvement at the state and county level, 1st paragraph; Table 3 (Mertz and Gill rows)
extracted: As summarized by the scoping review: in Allegheny County in 2008–2010, 66% of 112 unintentional deaths listing morphine but not heroin met criteria for heroin, and after review heroin-involved deaths rose from 171 to 245 while morphine-involved deaths fell from 132 to 41 and codeine-involved deaths from 34 to 5 (Mertz 2014); in New York City in 2006–2010, 84 of 118 deaths certified as acute opiate intoxication (71%) were attributed to heroin (Gill 2016). The primary studies were not read here. Editors' arithmetic: morphine/codeine decreases total (132−41)+(34−5)=120, versus 245−171=74 additional heroin deaths. The review does not reconcile this; overlapping drug categories are plausible, but no exclusive one-for-one recoding is established.

extracted: Second-hand in the scoping review: O'Donnell 2022 used SUDORS toxicology and scene evidence from 38 states and Washington DC, January 2018–December 2019. Among probable and suspected heroin-related overdose deaths, respectively 44.2% and 52.6% had only morphine on the death certificate; enhanced definitions raised the heroin-related share from 80.2% to 93.3%.
